newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK has tough line for firms at drought summit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK has tough line for firms at drought summit.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government took a tough line with water companies at a "crisis summit" on Monday, setting them stringent mandatory leakage targets as part of a 10-point plan to conserve supplies.
"I have asked (industry regulator Ofwat) to start immediately by setting demanding targets for next year as soon as possible," Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said.
Britain, traditionally seen as wet and rainy, is facing its worst drought for 200 years with rainfall well below average in most of the country.
But around 800 million gallons (3.6 billion litres) of water leaks out of the pipeline system every day, a figure which has outraged Labour politicians and consumer groups alike.
"It's (water) not being used efficiently and effectively and what we've got to do is bring in the proper regulatory form and to be quite tough with the industry," Prescott said.
Water companies, privatised by the former Conservative government in 1989, have incurred further public wrath by making soaring profits and padding executive pay packets and dividends.

The industry is already bracing itself for Labour's planned windfall tax on privatised utilities, aimed at funding a three billion pounds ($4.9 billion) plan to cut unemployment, although details have not yet been released.

The conference, which heard comments from companies, consumer groups, environmental lobbyists and regulators, was called to address water resource and supply problems after two years of below average rainfall.
Despite the tough government tone, delegates from all sides described the atmosphere as "harmonious," praising the opportunity to exchange widely differing views.
This year companies will try to cut leakage by 150 million gallons a day to conform with demands by regulator Ofwat.

Prescott said Ofwat head Ian Byatt had assured the government that his powers were enough to penalise companies which failed to meet targets. However, he added that the government had said "there might be more that may be needed. We will watch what happens over the summer."
Ofwat's powers include preventing price increases and it could seek authority to appoint an administrator in extreme circumstances.

Shares in water companies fell on the stock exchange following the conference, with Thames Water, which has one of the worst records on leaking pipes, down 11 pence by 1415 GMT to 671 pence per share and Severn Trent shedding 12.5 pence to 778.5 pence.

The industry maintains that it has spent over 500 million pounds on drought-related measures and is keen to follow a path of persuading customers to trim demand while at the same time planning additional resources such as reservoirs.
But Byatt warned the conference that there would be "no new resource developments...allowed until we are satisfied that leakage is at economic levels and that demand is being properly managed."

Environment minister Michael Meacher rejected compulsory metering of domestic customers but said there could be a case for selective metering of peak users, such as those with large gardens or swimming pools.
Ruth Evans, director of the National Consumer Council, warned that there were "limits to what consumers should or could be asked to do" to save water.

Prescott, who said he now cleans his teeth using a glass of water instead of a running tap, said simple measures such as plastic bags known as "hippos" placed in toilet cisterns to cut the amount of water used in flushing, could help to cut demand.
"Yes we'll have tough regulation of the water companies, but every one of us can play a part. So it's regulation and common sense -- together we can beat the drought," Prescott said.
Other proposals in the 10-point plan include a review of the charging system and that for abstraction, the process by which river water is diverted to supplies.
The government will also give water companies a statutory duty to conserve water in carrying out their functions and must ensure they promote efficient use of water by customers.
Prescott called on water companies to respond to the government's proposals within three weeks and suggested there could be a further conference in the autumn.
($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
